A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same title, authors, algorithms, and principal results. All 44 pages of each version, including Appendices A–E, are available and readable.

before.justification: v1 presents theoretical algorithms, bounds, and proofs. Neither the main text nor the appendices report original experiments, simulations, user studies, or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical. Its references to empirical learners concern mathematical learning models, not reported empirical experiments.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–7 retain the same inputs, steps, components, and parameter choices. The realizable learner, sanitization procedures, and private expert construction are unchanged.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or conducts training or evaluation experiments. The theoretical coverage of realizable and agnostic learning under adaptive and oblivious adversaries is unchanged.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally evaluates comparison methods. Existing theoretical comparisons are retained; the newly cited works are not added evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: No experimental protocols, data splits, evaluation metrics, training budgets, or testing procedures are reported in either version.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, empirical robustness tests, sensitivity studies, error analyses, or case studies. The appendices contain theoretical preliminaries, algorithms, and proofs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, empirical confidence intervals, or significance tests. The unchanged probability and concentration bounds are theoretical guarantees.

E6.justification: The paper's own results are unchanged, including the mistake, regret, and sample-complexity bounds throughout the main text and appendices. No empirical result entries are added or revised.

T1.justification: Footnote 3 attached to Lemma B.2 explicitly qualifies the privacy proof: the work requires stronger basic and advanced composition results valid for adaptive inputs, whereas classical composition concerns static datasets. This refines the formal justification without changing theorem statements, bounds, or the remaining derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same central claims: logarithmic realizable mistake bounds against adaptive adversaries and sublinear agnostic regret for Littlestone classes.

C2.justification: Section 5 adds a qualification to the question of improving the doubly exponential dependence on dimension: footnote 2 states that Lyu (2025) solved the realizable case against an oblivious adversary. This updates the scope of the remaining open question; other limitations and interpretations are unchanged.

D1.justification: Pseudocode, algorithm inputs, privacy parameters, and theoretical parameter prescriptions are retained. No implementation, hardware, runtime, code-access, or data-access information is added.

R1.justification: v2 adds Lyu (2025) on private learning of Littlestone classes and three composition references: Lyu (2022), Vadhan and Wang (2021), and Henzinger et al. (2025). These provide a limited update to research positioning and proof support.

P1.justification: Changes comprise two explanatory footnotes, an expanded affiliation for Bo Li, updated dates, and limited bibliographic edits. The section organization and substantive narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: The added footnotes and reference entries cause local reflow and changes in pseudocode placement, including Algorithm 4 moving from page 30 to page 31. No figures or tables are added, and the algorithm displays retain their content and styling.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the adaptive-input composition requirement explicit in Appendix B and updates Section 5 to acknowledge a solved special case of an open question. These improve precision and attribution, while the algorithms, guarantees, and substantive proofs remain otherwise unchanged.
